extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of classical essays and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted normative prescriptions and evaluative principles from Montaigne's Essays about prayer, religious writing, judgment of character, age, and vices — guidance for conduct and for assessing people and writings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve in writing of religion (for laity)
rubrics_metrics.description: An edict enjoining all people but such as are public professors of divinity to be very reserved in writing of religion would carry a good colour of utility and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues lay authors should avoid treating religious topics freely in print; theological exposition should be left mainly to public professors. He gives this as a prudential rule to prevent irreverence or error when the writer lacks proper authority or disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the name of God rarely and with reverence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even those not of our Church forbid the name of God to be used in common discourse, nor so much even by way of interjection, exclamation, assertion of a truth, or comparison; and I think them in the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke God only with the greatest reverence and devotion; avoid treating the divine name as everyday jargon or an emphatic filler. The surrounding examples contrast casual invocation with solemn prayer and emphasize appropriate solemnity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pray only with true devotion and proper disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hard to compose our souls to the calmness, patience, and devotion that a true prayer requires; otherwise our prayers are vain and even vicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prayer must be accompanied by repentance, a soul free from rancour, and genuine contrition. Invoking God in the midst of vice or mere habit is hypocritical — akin to calling a magistrate while committing a theft — and such prayers are unacceptable. Examples: prayers offered to support unjust designs or vices are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pray for everything you desire; pray for what is prudent
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not to pray that all things may go as we would have them, but as most concurrent with prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prayers should seek outcomes aligned with wisdom and the common good rather than private passions (covetousness, ambition, revenge). Montaigne illustrates how people invoke the divine to bless wicked designs; such use is criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: True prayer requires inward purity; public petitions can be suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: A true prayer and religious reconciling of ourselves to Almighty God cannot enter into an impure soul, subject at the very time to the dominion of Satan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against publicizing private prayers and notes that prayers uttered without inward repentance are 'guilty prayers.' He contrasts private devotion (sincere, inward) with ostentatious or hypocritical use of religious language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divine doctrine distinct and treated with special style
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine doctrine, as queen and regent of the rest, better keeps her state apart; she ought to be sovereign throughout, not subsidiary and suffragan, and grammatical, rhetorical, logical examples may elsewhere be more suitably chosen than from so sacred a matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theology should be handled in its own dignified manner; mixing theological matters casually into rhetorical or theatrical material lessens their reverence. Montaigne quotes authorities (St. Chrysostom) to support the claim that human eloquence should not appropriate the 'majesty of divine eloquence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should declare philosophical opinions as opinions, not as matters of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: I propose fancies merely human and merely my own, and that simply as human fancies, and separately considered, not as determined by any decree from heaven, matter of opinion, not matter of faith; things which I discourse of according to my own notions, not as I believe, according to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing on religious or metaphysical matters as a lay or philosopher, be explicit that you present personal, human conjectures and not doctrinal truths. Montaigne presents his essays as 'laical, not clerical' but still religious in tone; transparency about status of claims is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking divine aid for vicious ends (hypocrisy of wicked prayers)
rubrics_metrics.description: He who calls God to his assistance whilst in a course of vice, does as if a cut‑purse should call a magistrate to help him, or like those who introduce the name of God to the attestation of a lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne condemns prayers that sanctify or conceal immoral intentions; invoking the divine to enable theft, murder, or other crimes is morally perverse and will be judged accordingly (illustrated by classical and literary examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge character from isolated actions; require long-term constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a right judgment of a man, we are long and very observingly to follow his trace: if constancy does not there stand firm upon her own proper base...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character and virtue should be assessed by repeated, consistent behavior over time (constancy is the perfection of virtue). Single acts or sudden displays (bravery in one battle, a single compassionate act) are insufficient to ascribe a settled quality to a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy is the chief mark of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Demosthenes: 'the beginning of all virtue is consultation and deliberation; the end and perfection, constancy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses the classical idea that virtue culminates in constancy — willingness to will the same good consistently. Evaluate moral excellence by its permanence and integration into life, not by episodic actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge people by their ordinary, most usual behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: There seems some reason in forming a judgment of a man from the most usual methods of his life; the judgment would not be hard to make...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating persons, give greater weight to their typical, habitual comportment rather than exceptional moments. Montaigne warns against overvaluing rarity or novelty when assessing character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proximate circumstances when making judgments (avoid overgeneralizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The surest way to steer, in my opinion, would be to take our measures from the nearest allied circumstances, without engaging in a longer inquisition, or without concluding any other consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make practical judgments based on immediately relevant context; avoid extrapolating distant consequences or imposing a grand systematic rule where particular circumstances determine the appropriate response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ascribe a single, unitary character to people — expect internal variety
rubrics_metrics.description: I give to my soul sometimes one face and sometimes another... I have nothing to say of myself entirely, simply, and solidly without mixture and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne counsels humility in moral verdicts: people contain contradictory tendencies; evaluators should recognize internal plurality and not force a single label. This is both an epistemic and ethical recommendation in judging others and oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that some virtues can be produced by base motives (inspect motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since ambition can teach man valour, temperance, and liberality... 'tis not all the understanding has to do, simply to judge us by our outward actions; it must penetrate the very soul, and there discover by what springs the motion is guided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External virtuous acts may stem from ambition, avarice, or lust; assess underlying motives rather than solely visible deeds. Montaigne gives examples where vice produces apparent virtues (avarice producing courage, ambition producing generosity).

rubrics_metrics.name: True virtue must be pursued for itself, not borrowed as a mask
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue cannot be followed but for herself, and if one sometimes borrows her mask to some other purpose, she presently pulls it away again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether virtuous behavior is habitual and intrinsic. If virtue is merely a means to other ends, it will not endure; prefer actions done for their own sake when attributing moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conclude bravery from a single brave action; require universality of courage
rubrics_metrics.description: One gallant action, therefore, ought not to conclude a man valiant; if a man were brave indeed, he would be always so, and upon all occasions... he would bear a sickness in his bed as bravely as a wound in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bravery must be consistent across contexts (pavement and field, private and public); isolated courage can be situational (anger, company, wine) and should not define a person's enduring character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life is precarious; do not over-privilege an expected 'natural' old-age death
rubrics_metrics.description: To die of old age is a death rare, extraordinary, and singular... we ought rather... to call that natural which is general, common, and universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises realistic appraisal of life's fragility: plan and act without the illusion of a long natural life. Policies or personal plans that assume long life (delaying responsibility, postponing action) are criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society errs by delaying adult responsibilities; employ people earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fault in our very laws to maintain this error: these say that a man is not capable of managing his own estate till he be five-and-twenty years old... I should be of opinion that our vocation and employment should be as far as possible extended for the public good: I find the fault on the other side, that they do not employ us early enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legal and social age thresholds critically; Montaigne argues for earlier engagement in public and vocational duties (soul maturity at ~20) and criticizes extended apprenticeship/idle youth as wasteful given life's hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess natural gifts early; lack of early signs suggests permanency of defect
rubrics_metrics.description: For my part, I believe our souls are adult at twenty as much as they are ever like to be... The natural qualities and virtues produce what they have of vigorous and fine, within that term or never.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests that capacity and genius manifest early: when evaluating potential or suitability (for office, art, action), give weight to evidence produced by age twenty or thirty; absence of early signs often predicts lack of later emergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness is a particularly gross vice because it destroys reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Amongst the rest, drunkenness seems to me to be a gross and brutish vice... this one is totally corporeal and earthly... And the rudest nation this day in Europe is that alone where it is in fashion. Other vices discompose the understanding: this totally overthrows it and renders the body stupid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne ranks vices and singles out drunkenness as especially degrading because it obliterates reason and makes the body and soul stupid; in evaluation of moral seriousness, place drunkenness among the worst vices.
